Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:00 EST
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Lin (Redwood AE), Carlos Reyes (Redwood SE), Sara Mitchell (Head of AI, Valencia Bank), Daniel Cho (Infra Lead), Priya Raman (Security)

Summary:
Short discovery focused on Valencia Bank's needs for dedicated GPU capacity: isolation requirements, burst/scale behavior, expected throughput, and security/compliance constraints. Action items and next steps captured at end.

Topics:
- Current stack and where inference runs today
- Why dedicated vs hosted vs private for them
- Sizing, burst, and autoscaling expectations
- Security: SOC2, KMS, network isolation, audit logs
- Pilot/benchmark plan and timeline

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Jamie Lin: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Jamie, AE on the account, and with me is Carlos our SE. How are you all doing?
[00:05] Sara Mitchell: Doing good, Jamie. Thanks. We've been excited to talk through dedicated options.
[00:12] Carlos Reyes: Hey Sara, Daniel, Priya - quick agenda, we'll ask a few discovery q's then go into sizing and security. Sound good?
[00:18] Daniel Cho: Yep. We're hoping to understand how Redwood Dedicated would fit into our infra and costs.
[00:25] Priya Raman: And I want to dig into audit logs and KMS - must haves for us.
[00:34] Jamie Lin: Perfect. Quick opener - can you summarize where inference runs today and what models you're using?
[00:40] Sara Mitchell: So currently we run most inference on-prem on a mixed cluster - some VMs with NVIDIA A100s for heavy models and some lower-end gpus for lighter workloads. We're using a mix of open weights and some licensed models; latency SLAs vary by product. Sub-50ms isn't realistic across the board, but for our customer-facing chat, we want 200-400ms max.
[01:05] Daniel Cho: Right now we do manual scaling, spin up nodes overnight for batch jobs, but real-time is a pain, we hit noisy neighbor issues, and the ops burden is getting heavy. So isolation is key.
[01:20] Jamie Lin: Got it. So isolation + predictable throughput and cost. On the dedicated side we offer reserved GPU pools, dedicated to your tenancy with options for burst capacity - does that map to what you were thinking?
[01:34] Sara Mitchell: Yes. Two follow-ups: 1) what's the burst model look like, and 2) can we guarantee data never leaves our VPC?
[01:43] Carlos Reyes: For burst we support configurable burst capacity - you can reserve baseline nodes and then allow burst to a higher pool with pre-agreed limits. Billing for burst is typically a higher per-hour rate and can be capped. For VPC, our Private deployment is full customer-managed networking; Dedicated can be configured with VPC peering and strict egress rules. We also have on-prem appliance options for air-gapped if needed.
[02:05] Priya Raman: When you say VPC peering, is there any routing through Redwood-managed infra? We need to ensure keys never leave our KMS.
[02:14] Carlos Reyes: Good q. For Dedicated we support both peering and private link. Customer keys can be integrated with your KMS/HSM—Redwood will not persist plaintext keys. We can provide an integration guide.
[02:27] Daniel Cho: What's the typical CPU/GPU ratio for a Dedicated node? And how does autoscaling behave with stateful KV caches?
[02:36] Carlos Reyes: Nodes are typically one to two GPUs per host for low-latency inference; we provide tuning for batch sizes and concurrent streams. Autoscaling can be configured but warmup for large models needs KV cache priming. We do prefix/KV caching to reduce token cost, but if you scale out cold, you'll see initial latency spikes until cache warms. We can do pre-warming strategies during scale events.
[02:58] Sara Mitchell: That cache warm-up is a bit worrying. For our peak hours we need consistent latency; we can't have a flurry of cold starts.
[03:06] Jamie Lin: Totally understood. We recommend two levers: 1) reserved baseline capacity sized for steady-state QPS, and 2) short burst windows where you accept slightly higher billing but we keep a pool of warmed replicas. Also intelligent routing to keep session affinity to warmed nodes.
[03:26] Daniel Cho: How do we estimate baseline sizing? Our peak is around 450 concurrent chats, average request 150 tokens, 8 requests per minute per chat? (speaker pauses) math is fuzzy there.
[03:40] Carlos Reyes: Quick calc - rough qps: 450 * 8 / 60 = 60 QPS. Model latency per token matters; with a quantized Llama variant at 40ms per request median, you'd need X GPUs. We can run a benchmark with your payload to get real numbers.
[03:55] Sara Mitchell: We also have batch jobs overnight for fine-tuning and embeddings - those can use spare capacity or be scheduled on different pools?
[04:03] Jamie Lin: Yes, you can reserve pools by workload. Dedicated gives you multiple pools: low-latency pool pinned to small sequence lengths, and batch pool optimized for throughput. You can route jobs accordingly.
[04:15] Priya Raman: On compliance - SOC 2, ISO and audit logs - what's your retention and ability to provide per-request logs? We have auditors who will ask for that.
[04:24] Carlos Reyes: We emit detailed audit logs with per-request metadata; full payload logging is optional and can be disabled. Retention is configurable; enterprise packages include longer retention and log export to your SIEM via S3 or streaming. We'll share SOC2 docs after this call.
[04:40] Daniel Cho: Network-wise, firewall and port requirements? Our security team hates opening more holes than necessary.
[04:46] Jamie Lin: We'll provide a minimal network diagram. For VPC peering you only need egress to Redwood control plane for management; inference traffic can be kept on private paths. If you prefer, private deployment avoids routing through public internet.
[04:59] Sara Mitchell: Pricing orientation - is dedicated priced by GPU-hour + baseline commit? Any discounts for 12/24 month commitments?
[05:07] Jamie Lin: Yes, baseline committed capacity is billed monthly with discounts for 12/24 month terms. Burst is billed at an on-demand rate. We'll include example pricing tiers in the SOW.
[05:17] Priya Raman: Any third-party vendors involved or data shared with sub-processors? We need a list for our procurement.
[05:23] Carlos Reyes: We have cloud partners for hosted only; Dedicated contracts list our sub-processors. We'll provide the legal annex.
[05:31] Daniel Cho: If we do a pilot, how long to stand up a dedicated pool? We need to coordinate with infra changes for peering.
[05:38] Jamie Lin: Typical lead time is 2-3 weeks for Dedicated onboard including networking and SSO. Benchmarks can run in parallel once we have sample data.
[05:46] Sara Mitchell: For the benchmark - we want 95th percentile latency under 600ms for chat and throughput to sustain 60 QPS. Can Redwood do token-level cost estimates?
[05:55] Carlos Reyes: Yes, we provide token-level cost breakdowns after bench runs and suggestions on quantization/profiles to hit targets. We'll recommend model/quantization combos.
[06:05] Jamie Lin: Anything else on security or legal we should flag?
[06:09] Priya Raman: SSO/SAML support and granular RBAC are musts. Also searchable audit trails per user.
[06:16] Carlos Reyes: We support SAML/SCIM, and RBAC with per-route controls. Audit trails are exportable.
[06:23] Daniel Cho: Ok. On autoscaling - suppose we have a sudden traffic spike, how fast can you scale from baseline to burst? And do you have autoscaling policies based on queue depth or latency SLOs?
[06:33] Carlos Reyes: We offer policy-driven autoscaling; you can scale by target CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, or latency SLO. Cold start time depends on model size and cache; for small-medium models we can add nodes within a minute, large models could be a few minutes unless pre-warmed. That's why baseline sizing plus a warmed burst pool is recommended for production-critical routes.
[06:52] Sara Mitchell: That aligns with our thinking. Could you also walk us through failure modes? E.g., if a GPU drops, what's the fallback path?
[06:59] Jamie Lin: We have multi-zone placement and automatic failover to warm replicas. There's also model variant fallback - e.g., if highest perf model isn't available, route to a slightly cheaper/lower-latency variant to maintain availability. You control fallback policies.
[07:14] Priya Raman: For encryption at rest, do you support customer-managed keys for persistent caches?
[07:20] Carlos Reyes: Yes, encryption at rest with CMKs is supported for caches and stored artifacts. Keys never leave your KMS.
[07:26] Sara Mitchell: Great. Let's talk about timeline - if we start a pilot now, can we be production-ready in Q2? (she laughs)
[07:34] Jamie Lin: Q2 is realistic assuming procurement + networking moves quickly. We'll follow up with a project plan in the SOW.
[07:41] Daniel Cho: One more infra detail - what's your telemetry footprint? We need to ensure agents don't send PII offsite.
[07:48] Carlos Reyes: Telemetry is configurable. By default we collect metrics and traces. You can disable payload capture. We can provide a telemetry whitelist for only non-sensitive metrics.
[07:57] Sara Mitchell: Okay sounds good. Any competitors we should be aware of? We're evaluating Anthropic's enterprise offering and AWS Bedrock for hosted / managed endpoints.
[08:06] Jamie Lin: Understood. Redwood's differentiator here is the unified runtime across Hosted/Dedicated/Private and the production-first tooling - e.g., cost/latency dashboards and rollout policies.
[08:16] Priya Raman: For procurement, send a standard MSA and any addenda about data residency.
[08:21] Jamie Lin: Will do. We'll include the legal annex and sub-processor list.
[08:26] Carlos Reyes: Next steps recap: we'll send pricing + SOW, SOC2/ISO artifacts, and coordinate benchmark dataset and kickoff.
[08:34] Sara Mitchell: Perfect. Thanks. I'll get the sample queries to you by next Tuesday.
[08:39] Jamie Lin: Thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark kickoff and the SOW.
[08:44] End of call.
